client: I've been feeling really anxious about this networking event I have to attend next week. Just thinking about it makes my heart race because I know I'll have to introduce myself to strangers in my field. I can't shake the feeling that I'm going to embarrass myself or that no one will want to talk to me. Honestly, I'm not sure if therapy can really help with this.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel anxious about networking events, especially when you’re anticipating interactions with new people. Your feelings of worry about embarrassment and being ignored are valid, and it's okay to express that uncertainty about therapy too. What do you think might happen if you challenged those thoughts about introducing yourself?

client: I guess if I tried to challenge those thoughts, I might realize that not everyone is judging me as harshly as I think they are. But honestly, it's hard for me to imagine things going well. I always picture the worst-case scenario, like stumbling over my words or just standing there awkwardly while everyone else seems to connect effortlessly. I just don’t know if I can really change that mindset in time for the event.
therapist: It's great that you can recognize that not everyone is judging you as harshly as you fear. Imagining worst-case scenarios can be very common, but it can also limit your perspective. What if you tried to create a more balanced view by thinking about times when you've connected well with others, or even considering that the event might not go as badly as you imagine?

client: I see what you're saying about trying to think of times I’ve connected with others, but it’s tough for me to remember those moments when I’m so focused on the anxiety. I guess I have had some good conversations before, but they feel so far away from what I’m facing now. I’m just worried that even if I try to think positively, my nerves will still get the better of me at the event.
therapist: It’s completely understandable to feel overwhelmed by anxiety when it feels so present, making it hard to recall those positive experiences. It’s normal for nerves to be part of the equation, but they don’t have to define your experience at the event. What if you set a small goal for yourself, like starting a conversation with just one person? How might that shift your focus and help ease some of that anxiety?

client: I can see how starting with just one conversation might make it feel less overwhelming, but I still worry that I won't even be able to approach someone. What if I try to talk to someone and it goes poorly? It feels like there's so much pressure to make that one interaction go well, and I just don't know if I can handle that kind of pressure right now.
therapist: It's understandable to feel pressure around making that first interaction go well, especially when anxiety is high. Remember that it's okay to have a conversation that feels a bit awkward or doesn't go as planned; it doesn't reflect your worth or abilities. How about considering that each interaction is a learning experience, and what if you approached it with curiosity rather than pressure? What might that look like for you?

client: I get what you're saying about approaching it with curiosity, but it feels hard to shift my mindset like that at the moment. I keep thinking about how much I want to make a good impression, and that makes it hard to see it as just a learning experience. What if I end up feeling more embarrassed than I would have if I just didn’t go at all?
therapist: It's completely valid to feel the weight of wanting to make a good impression, and it’s understandable that this pressure can make a learning mindset feel elusive. It’s also okay to acknowledge the fear of embarrassment; that’s a common concern in social situations. If you decided to go, what small steps might you take to ease the pressure on yourself, perhaps by focusing on simply enjoying the experience rather than worrying about the outcome?

client: I think focusing on enjoying the experience sounds nice in theory, but it feels really hard to do in practice. I keep getting caught up in my thoughts about what people will think of me, and I don’t know how to just let that go. Maybe if I had a specific plan or something to distract me, that would help, but I’m not sure what that would even look like at this point.
therapist: It makes sense that focusing on enjoying the experience feels difficult when your thoughts are so loud and persistent. Creating a specific plan can definitely help provide a sense of direction and ease some of that anxiety. What if you brainstormed a few conversation starters or even set a goal to find someone with a shared interest? How might having a plan like that influence your confidence or help you feel more prepared?

client: I can see how having some conversation starters could help me feel a bit more prepared, but honestly, it feels daunting to come up with those on my own. I worry that if I try to think of something and it doesn’t go well, it’ll just add to my anxiety instead of helping. What if I forget what I planned to say in the moment? It feels like a lot of pressure to come up with the right words when I'm already feeling so anxious.
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel daunted by the idea of coming up with conversation starters, especially when anxiety is already high. The pressure to remember everything can feel overwhelming. What if you approached it as a flexible guide rather than a strict plan? You could jot down just a few key phrases or topics that feel comfortable to you, knowing that it's okay to adapt in the moment. How does that idea resonate with you?

client: I guess thinking of it as a flexible guide makes it feel a little less intimidating, but I still worry that I won’t be able to think on my feet. What if the conversation turns in a direction I didn’t prepare for, and I just freeze up? It feels like even having a few phrases might not be enough to help me feel more confident, especially when my anxiety kicks in.
therapist: It's completely normal to feel anxious about unexpected turns in a conversation, and it’s okay to recognize that you might freeze up in those moments. It might help to remind yourself that many people experience similar feelings, and it’s natural for conversations to flow in different directions. What if you allowed yourself to embrace the uncertainty, focusing on being present rather than striving for perfection? How might that shift in perspective change how you approach the event?

client: I can see how embracing uncertainty could help me feel a bit more relaxed, but it’s still really hard to let go of that pressure to be perfect. I keep thinking about how I want to make a good impression, and it feels like I’d just be setting myself up for disappointment if I don’t manage to do that. What if I end up feeling more anxious or embarrassed instead of actually enjoying the event?
therapist: It's completely understandable to feel that pressure to make a good impression, and it's natural to worry about the possibility of feeling disappointed. Remember, though, that every experience, even the challenging ones, can offer valuable insights and growth. What if you considered the event as an opportunity for exploration rather than a test of your worth? How might that shift your focus and allow you to engage more freely?

client: I can see how thinking of the event as an opportunity for exploration could take some pressure off, but it's still hard to shake off that feeling of needing to prove myself. I worry that if I don't impress anyone, it’ll just reinforce my feelings of anxiety and loneliness. I guess I just have a hard time picturing myself being open and engaging when I feel so much pressure to perform.
therapist: It's completely valid to feel that pressure to prove yourself, and it's understandable that you're concerned about how it might impact your feelings of anxiety and loneliness. It might help to remind yourself that everyone at the event is human, often feeling their own nervousness and self-doubt. What if you allowed yourself to simply be present and share your genuine self, focusing on connecting with others rather than impressing them? How do you think that shift could influence your experience?
